hypothesis: Simple NFC/lowercase alias detection might miss final sigma/dotless i/long s/micro sign collisions on Windows; broader uppercase-then-lowercase folding was considered.
finding: Hypothesis contradicted by native probes on this host. Both case-insensitive C and D directories preserve all six suspected pairs distinctly, while three ordinary ASCII/Greek case controls collide. No broader folding was added.

native.scope: Current C/D directory controls only. Native directory enumeration retained; no file payload/device/overwrite/deletion. Other Windows hosts/volumes remain unverified.

tests.behavior: Archive create/extract preserves two different byte payloads under exact original names. Selected handles prepare a large virtual stream whose metadata and payload reads preserve both names and exact bytes. Native alias controls reject before preparation.
tests.mutation: Isolated archive module copy changes NFC/lowercase aliases to uppercase-then-lowercase expansion; six legal-name tests fail and three alias controls pass. Mutant excluded from normal tests by validation-only location, no production mutation.

validation.dependencies: Existing fresh stage/unchanged lock; no new npmci.
validation.browserScope: Prior88Edge/88Chrome gates retain current app/server/runtime/build byte scope; test-only addition, no browser rerun. Native/default-handler/CMD limitations retained.

limitations: Only one Windows host/two local directories; directory behavior does not exhaust filesystem/volume/OS Unicode tables or native picker/file-write semantics.
Existing portable guard can be stricter than these local directories for NFC/lowercase-equivalent names. No attempt to loosen portable-name policy.
No data payload was written by native directory probes; no device file opened, data overwrite, cleanup, or preserved-data deletion.
The negative-control algorithm is a deliberately bad uppercase-expansion candidate, not a claim about every Unicode case-fold algorithm.
